nameStory: The "tiny many-spored buttons" name perfectly captures this lichen's appearance and reproductive strategy. Like miniature shirt buttons scattered across bark, these small circular lichens are packed with an unusually high number of spores compared to their relatives. The "many-spored" part refers to their asci (spore sacs) containing more than the typical eight spores found in most lichens.
description: Tiny Many-spored Buttons is a crustose lichen that forms small, dark, button-like structures on tree bark. This inconspicuous organism creates a symbiotic partnership between fungi and algae, appearing as tiny black dots scattered across its host surface. Individual "buttons" are typically less than 2mm across, making them easy to overlook without close inspection. The lichen forms thin, often barely visible crusts with the distinctive dark fruiting bodies (apothecia) that give it its common name.

idTips.label: Button-like fruiting bodies
idTips.description: Look for tiny, perfectly round, black dots that feel slightly raised when you run your finger gently across the bark - like miniature buttons sewn onto the surface

idTips.label: Size and arrangement
idTips.description: Individual buttons are pinhead-small, typically 1-2mm across, scattered sparsely rather than clustered together

idTips.label: Surface texture
idTips.description: The buttons have a matte, non-reflective black surface that feels firm and slightly granular to gentle touch

idTips.label: Surrounding crust
idTips.description: The background lichen body is often barely visible as a thin, pale gray to whitish film that may be almost imperceptible

idTips.label: Host preference
idTips.description: Found exclusively on bark that feels smooth to moderately textured, never on rough or deeply furrowed bark surfaces

habitat: This lichen favors the smooth to moderately textured bark of deciduous trees, particularly maples, birches, and younger oaks in New England's mixed forests. It thrives in areas with good air circulation and moderate light levels, often found at eye level on tree trunks in woodlands and forest edges. You're most likely to spot it in relatively unpolluted areas away from heavy traffic or industrial activity.

seasonality.spring: Fruiting bodies become more prominent as humidity increases, making the dark buttons easier to spot against the lighter bark. This is an excellent time for identification as the contrast is strongest.
seasonality.summer: The lichen may appear less obvious during dry periods, with buttons seeming to shrink slightly. Look for them during humid mornings when they're most visible.
seasonality.fall: Autumn moisture makes identification easier again, and falling leaves expose more bark surface for searching. The buttons remain clearly visible against wet bark.
seasonality.winter: Snow and ice may obscure the tiny buttons, but they remain present year-round. Check south-facing tree trunks where snow melts first for winter observations.

funFact: Despite being called "many-spored," each tiny button can release hundreds of thousands of microscopic spores into the air - so many that if you could see them all at once, it would look like the tree was smoking!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with small insect eggs, bird droppings, or other dark crustose lichens. Unlike insect eggs, these buttons are rock-hard and permanently attached - you can't scrape them off with your fingernail. Remember: "Buttons stay put, bugs brush away."
contextualKnowledge: The rarity of this species in New England (with only one recorded observation) means any sighting would be scientifically valuable. Many amateur naturalists overlook crustose lichens entirely, focusing on the showier leafy and shrubby types, but these "microlichens" represent the vast majority of lichen diversity.
compareHints: Tiny Many-spored Buttons differs from its relative Tiny Button Lichen mainly in spore characteristics that require microscopic examination - field identification between these species is nearly impossible without laboratory work. Both appear as small dark buttons on bark, but the many-spored species tends to have slightly more scattered, less numerous fruiting bodies. When in doubt, detailed photography and expert consultation are needed for definitive identification.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Tiny Button Lichen differs from its relative Tiny Many-spored Buttons by having fewer spores in each reproductive disc and typically smaller, more numerous buttons.
Compared to its close relative Tiny Button Lichen (Amandinea punctata), milliaria tends to have more numerous reproductive structures giving it that "thousand dots" appearance that inspired its name.
